seoTitle: Michigan Spinal Cord Injury Lawyer – Paralysis & Spine Injury Claims
seoDescription: A spinal cord injury costs $2 million to $6 million over a lifetime. Michigan no-fault can pay for it, within limits set in 2019. ATLAW explains benefits, the threshold, and disc-injury defenses. Free review.
tagline: The first year of a high spinal cord injury costs more than most insurance policies hold. The case is about where the rest comes from.

c.v: A spinal cord injury is the injury Michigan’s no-fault system was built for. The first year after a high cervical injury costs about $1.37 million in care and equipment; every year after costs about $238,000; over the life of a 25-year-old, about $6 million. Those figures, from the National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, are why Michigan drivers were required to carry unlimited lifetime medical coverage for 46 years, and why the 2019 decision to let drivers buy less has consequences that arrive in a hospital room.

Spinal injury cases in Michigan range from complete paralysis after a rollover to a herniated cervical disc after a rear-end crash that ends a tradesman’s career. Both are spine cases; both meet Michigan’s injury threshold when properly documented; and both are defended the same way, by calling the injury pre-existing, degenerative, or exaggerated. This page explains what no-fault pays for a spinal cord injury and where the limits are, how the threshold applies to paralysis and to disc injuries, how the degenerative-condition defense is answered, what the lifetime numbers mean for the claim against the at-fault party, and the deadlines.

sections.heading: Kinds of spinal injury, and why the classification matters

c.v: Physicians classify a spinal cord injury by level (cervical C1–C8, thoracic T1–T12, lumbar L1–L5, sacral) and by completeness on the ASIA Impairment Scale: A (complete, no motor or sensory function below the level), B through D (incomplete, with increasing preserved function), and E (normal). Tetraplegia (quadriplegia) involves the arms and legs; paraplegia the legs and trunk. The level and grade determine the care plan, the equipment, and the lifetime cost, and they are the foundation of the life care plan that converts a medical prognosis into a damages number.

Spine injuries without cord damage are far more common and no less real: herniated and ruptured discs with nerve root compression (radiculopathy), vertebral fractures, spondylolisthesis, and injuries requiring fusion or disc replacement surgery. They are proved with MRI, EMG and nerve conduction studies, surgical findings, and the treating surgeon’s causation opinion, and they are the spine cases most often contested on the ground discussed below.

sections.heading: The injury threshold: paralysis, and herniated discs

c.v: To recover pain and suffering from the at-fault driver in a crash, your injury must be a serious impairment of body function, permanent serious disfigurement, or death (MCL 500.3135(1)). The test, from McCormick v Carrier (2010) and now in the statute (500.3135(5)): an objectively manifested impairment of an important body function that affects the person’s general ability to lead his or her normal life, with no requirement of permanence. Paralysis satisfies every element on the medical record alone. A disc herniation satisfies the first element through imaging and clinical findings, the second because the spine’s function is important, and the third through the documented change in work, activity, and daily life; it is the third element insurers contest, with surveillance and with the argument that the claimant “can still do most things.” Fault above 50% bars pain and suffering (500.3135(2)(b)); fault below reduces it. Spinal injuries from falls, assaults, products, and medical errors carry no threshold.

Nearly every adult over 30 has some disc degeneration on MRI, and insurers in spine cases argue that the herniation was pre-existing and the crash did nothing. Michigan law answers it two ways. A defendant takes the plaintiff as found: aggravation of a pre-existing condition is compensable, and a crash that turns an asymptomatic degenerated disc into a symptomatic herniation requiring surgery caused that injury. And the comparison is made with evidence: prior medical records showing no treatment or complaints, pre- and post-crash imaging read side by side by a radiologist, the treating surgeon’s opinion on acute versus chronic findings (such as edema, annular tears, and fracture lines), and the timeline of symptoms from the emergency room forward. The cases that lose this argument are the ones where the record was not built: a gap in treatment, no imaging for months, and an emergency room note that says “back pain, no acute findings.”

sections.heading: What no-fault pays for a spinal cord injury

c.v: Michigan PIP benefits are paid by your own insurer, a household insurer, or the Assigned Claims Plan regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107, 500.3114), with written notice within one year (500.3145). For a spinal cord injury the categories that matter:

sections.heading: Spinal injuries from falls, diving, violence, and medical care

c.v: Crashes cause 37.5% of spinal cord injuries; falls cause 31.7%, and the share rises with age. A fall from a ladder, a scaffold, a deck, or down a stairway is a premises or construction case with no threshold requirement and, since 2023, no “open and obvious” dismissal (Kandil-Elsayed v F & E Oil). Diving injuries at pools, lakes, and quarries, a summer pattern in Michigan, turn on depth markings, warnings, and supervision. Violence accounts for 15.4%, raising negligent security claims against the property where it occurred. faqs.question: How much does a spinal cord injury cost over a lifetime?

answer.v: According to the National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center, from about $1.4 million (ASIA D, injured at 50) to about $6.1 million (high tetraplegia, injured at 25), excluding lost wages. The first year alone runs from $447,000 to $1.37 million.

faqs.question: Will Michigan no-fault pay for lifetime care?

answer.v: Up to your PIP medical limit. Unlimited coverage pays for life; $500,000 or $250,000 does not come close in a tetraplegia case. Care beyond the limit is claimed from the at-fault party and from health insurance and Medicaid.

faqs.question: Does a herniated disc meet the serious impairment threshold?

answer.v: It can. A herniation documented by MRI and clinical findings is objectively manifested; the spine is an important body function; and the question is whether it affected your general ability to lead your normal life (McCormick v Carrier, 2010). Surgery, work restrictions, and documented changes in activity carry the point.

faqs.question: The insurer says my disc problems are “degenerative.” What now?

answer.v: Aggravation of a pre-existing condition is compensable in Michigan. The answer is prior records showing no symptoms, side-by-side imaging, and the treating surgeon’s opinion on acute findings. Build the record early.

faqs.question: How many hours of attendant care will no-fault pay?

answer.v: Family-provided care is capped at 56 hours a week for crashes on or after June 11, 2019 (MCL 500.3157(10)); agency care covers the rest at the fee-schedule rate. People injured before that date have no cap (Andary v USAA, 2023).

faqs.question: Will no-fault pay for a wheelchair-accessible van and home modifications?

answer.v: Modifications reasonably necessary for your care and recovery are allowable expenses; the extent, especially for the vehicle itself and for a new residence, is governed by case law your lawyer will apply to your facts.

faqs.question: Can I recover lost wages for life?

answer.v: Three years of wage loss from no-fault (85%, capped monthly); lost earning capacity beyond that from the at-fault party as excess economic damages, projected by a vocational economist.

faqs.question: I was paralyzed in a fall at work. Who pays?

answer.v: Workers’ compensation pays medical care and wage benefits regardless of fault (MCL 418.301). A lawsuit against anyone other than your employer, such as a scaffold or ladder manufacturer, a property owner, or another contractor, recovers the rest.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on damages?

answer.v: Not in crash, premises, or workplace third-party cases. Medical malpractice and product liability cases are capped for non-economic damages at $1,065,000 in 2026 where the injury caused permanent loss of a vital bodily function.

One year for the no-fault notice; three years for the lawsuit against the at-fault party or a product maker; two years for medical malpractice; 90 days to notify an employer of a work injury; and 60 to 120 days to notify a government defendant.
